channel.title: Aaron Stalberg — writing on AI search visibility and automation
channel.description: Articles by Aaron Stalberg on how AI systems decide what to show people, why they prefer stale sources over accurate ones, and what goes wrong when AI automation has to run every day.

item.title: How AI assistants choose which sources to believe
item.description: An assistant answering a question about your category is not ranking pages, it is deciding which sources to trust. What actually gets picked, why vague pages are useless to it, and why the same facts produce different answers in different assistants.

item.title: Mentioned is not the same as cited
item.description: Being in the answer and being the reason for the answer are two different outcomes, and only one of them compounds. How to tell which one you are, and what moves you from mentioned to cited.

item.title: The same question to five AI engines, five different answers
item.description: I put one buying question to five assistants on the same day. Different companies named, different sources cited, and occasional disagreement about facts. What the spread between engines tells you, and how to run the test yourself.

item.title: What happens when nobody is left to correct the source
item.description: An AI answer is a summary of sources that were correct once. When the publisher folds, the archive closes, or the record is deleted, a wrong answer has nothing left to correct it, and no appeal process exists.

item.title: How to check in one afternoon whether AI knows your business exists
item.description: A free, manual method: ten buyer questions, four assistants, one spreadsheet. You will probably find you are named less often than you assumed, and that the sources driving the answers are not the pages you have been optimising.

item.title: Why “just fix the website” does not fix AI visibility
item.description: I measured 37 sites. Domain authority, traffic and a well-built homepage did not predict whether an assistant named them. What did was how describable the company was, and how consistently that description appeared off the site.

item.title: Why most AI automation projects fail in month four
item.description: Almost every AI automation works in the demo. The failures happen later, and they are predictable: no named owner once the build is finished, drift in the inputs nobody monitors, unhandled exceptions that silently drop work, and nobody watching the thing run. Six failure modes and the cheap fix for each.

item.title: When an AI gets you wrong, the problem is upstream
item.description: The assistant is not lying about you. It is accurately repeating something inaccurate that it found, and it has no reason to prefer your own account over a source it already trusts. Why correcting an AI's output achieves almost nothing, and correcting the source achieves a great deal.

item.title: Your business is missing from AI answers, and you would not know
item.description: Ask an assistant to recommend a supplier in most categories and you get a short list of three to five names. The person asking treats that list as the answer. If your business is not on it, the enquiry never reaches you, and no analytics tool reports the loss.

item.title: Why I gave $8,000 to a stranger's mission trip
item.description: She raised $8,185 from eleven people. I was $8,000 of it. What I think giving is actually for, and why the reasoning matters more than the amount.
